docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the hardware design, PCB layout, component selection, and embedded C firmware for a low-power environmental monitoring node. It serves as a clear technical guide for building, programming, and testing the system.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
This repository contains my individual subsystem for our team's EGR304 Embedded Systems Design project. My system monitors real-time environmental data—including atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and ambient light levels—using a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller.

The module processes sensor data, displays values on an LCD screen, and sends live data over UART to a central display. It runs on a custom regulated power circuit designed for efficiency and reliable operation.

For full context on how this node integrates into our overall system, see our Team Report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I designed and built this subsystem from circuit concept to hardware testing. Key contributions include:

  • Schematic Design: Created KiCad schematics using US symbol standards for the power regulator, sensors, and display interfaces.
  • PCB Layout: Completed component placement, signal routing, DRC verification, and Gerber file generation for manufacturing.
  • Firmware Development: Wrote C code in MPLAB X IDE for the PIC18F57Q43, featuring a multi-sample rolling buffer for digital signal smoothing and UART data output.
  • Hardware Validation: Tested power rails and verified sensor data output using an oscilloscope and digital multimeter.

docs.title: Subsystem Overview
docs.text: This custom 2-layer printed circuit board (PCB) was designed for the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano subsystem. The board features standard \(0.2\text{ mm}\) signal traces, \(0.4\text{ mm}\) \(+5\text{V}\) power distribution rails, dual top and bottom ground planes (F.Cu and B.Cu), and custom knockout copper text for top/bottom layer identification and compliance.

docs.title: Purpose of the Block Diagram
docs.text: The purpose of this individual subsystem block diagram is to define the hardware layout, signal conditioning stages, and electrical interfaces for the light-sensing subsystem prior to schematic capture and PCB layout. It serves as a visual guide for component selection, pin mapping on the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller, voltage management, and inter-board connectivity with teammates' hardware.

docs.title: System Specifications & Key Features
docs.text:
• Power Source & Supply Voltage: The subsystem is powered by a regulated +5V DC power domain capable of delivering up to 1.5A via an LM7805 linear voltage regulator. This rail powers the microcontroller, analog signal conditioning components, and sensor interface.

  • Power Levels: All signal levels operating within this block maintain a nominal voltage range of 0 to 5V DC across both analog input paths and digital serial communication lines.

  • Sensor & Signal Conditioning:

  • Sensor: A 5540 photoresistor configured in a voltage divider continuously measures ambient light levels.

  • Signal Conditioning: The variable analog output from the photoresistor passes through a Microchip MCP6004 operational amplifier configured as a non-inverting buffer. This stage provides high input impedance to prevent loading on the sensor divider and low output impedance to cleanly drive the microcontroller's RA0 ADC pin.

  • Team Connections & Communication Interfaces: Inter-board connectivity and system-wide integration are handled through standard ribbon cable connector Connector 1:

  • Digital Serial (UART): Transmit (TX on pin RC2) and Receive (RX on pin RC3) signals interface with teammates' boards via dedicated 5V UART lines at pins 2 and 3 of Connector 1.
  • Shared Ground & Power: Pin 8 of Connector 1 establishes a common ground (GND) across all team boards to maintain a consistent signal reference.

docs.title: Component Selection: Light Sensing Subsystem
docs.text: This document identifies, compares, and contrasts multiple off-the-shelf and custom solutions for every major active component in the Light Sensing Subsystem.

docs.title: Light Sensor / Photoresistor
docs.text:
• Subsystem: Light Sensing Subsystem
  • Description: A variable resistor whose resistance decreases with increasing incident light intensity, used to detect ambient light levels.

Option 1: Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103 Photoresistor - Unit Cost: $0.72 - Pros: * Industry-standard component with well-documented spectral response matching human eye adaptation (~520 nm peak) * Reliable 16–33 kΩ resistance range at 10 lux for clear voltage divider scaling * Simple passive two-terminal through-hole interface requiring minimal board space - Cons: * Contains cadmium sulfide (CdS), which is subject to environmental regulatory restrictions in certain regions * Slower response time compared to semiconductor photodiodes * Performance varies noticeably across operating temperature ranges

Option 2: Adafruit Industries LLC Photoresistor (161)

- Unit Cost: $0.95 - Pros: * Easily accessible hobbyist and prototyping component with broad community documentation * Standard through-hole leads fit standard breadboards and perfboards seamlessly * Cost-effective solution for basic light-level detection - Cons: * Lacks detailed, rigorous industrial datasheet parametric curves for precise engineering calculations * Part-to-part manufacturing tolerances can be wider than industrial-grade components

Option 3: Advanced Photonix NSL-19M51 Photoresistor - Unit Cost: $1.05 - Pros: * Tight resistance tolerance band for more predictable circuit response * Optimized peak spectral response closely mimicking human eye perception * High-reliability hermetic or robust package construction suitable for semi-industrial environments - Cons: * Higher unit cost compared to standard commercial CdS cells * Slower dark-to-light transition times under low illumination levels

Choice: Option 1: Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103 Photoresistor Rationale: We went with this photoresistor because it's widely used, easy to find data on, and gives us a very reliable resistance change when room lighting shifts. Plus, its through-hole leads make it super easy to mount right up against our enclosure window without needing any adapters.

docs.title: Signal Conditioning / Operational Amplifier
docs.text:
• Subsystem: Light Sensing Subsystem
  • Description: Active multi-channel integrated circuit used to buffer, scale, and condition the analog voltage signal from the photoresistor divider before routing it to the microcontroller ADC.

Option 1: Microchip Technology MCP6004-I/P Quad Op-Amp - Unit Cost: $0.60 - Pros: * Quad packaging provides four independent amplifiers in a single 14-pin DIP package, matching multi-channel project needs * Rail-to-rail input and output voltage capability maximizes ADC dynamic range * Extremely low quiescent supply current (~100 µA per channel) ideal for efficient power budgets - Cons: * Modest 1 MHz Gain Bandwidth Product limits high-frequency filtering applications * Higher input offset voltage (4.5 mV max) compared to precision zero-drift amplifiers

Option 2: Texas Instruments LM324AN/NOPB Quad Operational Amplifier - Unit Cost: \(1.18 - **Pros:** * Industry classic, highly robust, and widely second-sourced across manufacturers * Operates on a wide single-supply voltage range with low unit cost * Readily available through-hole PDIP package for straightforward prototyping - **Cons:** * Outputs do not comfortably reach ground (\)V_{ss}$) without a pull-down resistor on single-supply setups * Higher input bias currents can introduce loading errors on high-impedance resistive sensors

Option 3: Texas Instruments LM2904N/NOPB Dual Operational Amplifier - Unit Cost: $1.53 - Pros: * Proven automotive/industrial grade dual op-amp with robust temperature stability * Low input bias current and low quiescent power consumption * Standard 8-pin DIP package is compact and easy to solder - Cons: * Only contains two operational amplifiers per package, requiring multiple ICs if extra channels are needed * Slower slew rate compared to modern CMOS operational amplifiers

Choice: Option 1: Microchip Technology MCP6004-I/P Quad Op-Amp Rationale: The MCP6004 is great because it has rail-to-rail inputs and outputs, meaning our signal can go all the way from 0V to 5V without getting cut off or clipped by the chip. Having four amps in one package also gives us extra room to work with if we need to expand our circuit later.

docs.title: Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
• Subsystem: Power Distribution / Light Sensing Subsystem
  • Description: Linear voltage regulator used to step down an external DC input voltage to a stable +5V rail for system logic and active sensors.

Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV Linear Regulator - Unit Cost: $1.08 - Pros: * Built-in internal thermal overload and short-circuit current limiting protections * Industry-standard TO-220 package allows easy attachment to a heatsink if dissipation increases * Requires very few external support components (simple input/output bypass capacitors) - Cons: * Low power efficiency when dropping high input voltages down to 5V (linear voltage drop is lost as heat) * Higher dropout voltage requires at least 7V–7.5V input to guarantee solid 5V regulation

Option 2: Fairchild Semiconductor LM7805CT Linear Regulator - Unit Cost: $1.74 - Pros: * Classic 1.5A positive voltage regulator design with robust transient response * Standard pinout compatible with universal TO-220 layouts * Well-established thermal and electrical safety characteristics - Cons: * Stock availability can fluctuate depending on manufacturer lot allocations * Standard linear thermal dissipation constraints apply under heavy load differences

Option 3: UMW L7805CV Linear Regulator - Unit Cost: $1.74 - Pros: * Highly economical pricing for budget-conscious project builds * Standard TO-220 packaging for easy mounting and prototyping * Provides stable fixed 5V output for standard logic and sensor rails - Cons: * Alternative second-source brand with less historical pedigree than tier-1 manufacturers like STMicroelectronics * Maximum output current is rated slightly lower or subject to variance compared to classic 1.5A variants

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV Linear Regulator Rationale: We chose the STMicro regulator because it's a dependable, standard part that gives us a clean 5V output without adding switching noise to our sensitive analog sensor lines. The TO-220 package also makes it simple to mount and handle during testing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This repository contains the individual ECAD schematic design for the Light-Sensing Subsystem developed using KiCad for the EGR 304 engineering design project. The subsystem integrates power regulation, microcontroller interfacing, analog signal conditioning, and debugging hardware around a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano platform.

docs.title: Functional Subsystems
docs.text:
• Power Regulation Subsystem
  • Accepts external input (9V–$12V) via a through-hole Barrel Jack (J2) protected by a 500 mA inline fuse (F1).

  • Utilizes input (\(0.33\text{ }\mu\text{F}\)) and output (\(0.1\text{ }\mu\text{F}\)) filtering capacitors alongside an LM7805 linear regulator (U3) and a 100 \(\Omega\) preload resistor (R3) to establish a stable \(5\text{ V}\) rail.

  • Microcontroller Unit (MCU)

  • Implemented using a custom-designed PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano symbol (U1) featuring proper decoupling capacitance (C3) and dedicated UART communication routing (CDC_RX, CDC_TX) for upstream/downstream interfacing.

  • Light Sensor & Signal Conditioning Subsystem

  • Employs a photoresistor voltage divider (R1, R2) to detect ambient light.

  • Conditions the analog signal through an MCP6004 quad operational amplifier configured as a unity-gain buffer (U2A), with unused channels safely terminated.

  • User Interface & Debugging Subsystem

  • Includes a power-status indicator LED (D1, \(330\text{ }\Omega\) resistor R6) and a microcontroller-driven debug LED (D2 on RA1, \(330\text{ }\Omega\) resistor R7).
  • Features an active-low pushbutton (SW1 on RA2) with a \(10\text{ k}\Omega\) pull-up resistor (R8) for testing and user input.
  • Interfaces with external hardware and signals via a dedicated ribbon cable connector (J1).

docs.title: What I Did
docs.text: I created a complete power budget for my Light Sensing Subsystem by breaking down every active component and tracking how power flows through the system: 1. Listed Active Components: I identified my microcontroller, op-amp, and photoresistor as the core power consumers, recording their exact maximum current draws from my design. 2. Calculated Rail Requirements: I consolidated everything onto a single +5V power rail, added a 25% safety buffer, and calculated a total required active current of 28.125 mA. 3. Selected Voltage Regulation & Power Source: I chose the L7805CV linear regulator to step down a 9V DC wall adapter (WSU090-1300-13), ensuring clean, low-ripple analog power with plenty of headroom. 4. Projected Battery Life: I calculated the estimated continuous runtime (around 21.33 hours using a 480 mAh 9V battery) should I ever choose to run the circuit portably during testing.

docs.title: Why I Did a Power Budget
docs.text: A power budget is a critical step in engineering design for several reasons: * Prevents Component Failure: It guarantees that my power supplies, regulators, and wall adapters can deliver enough current without overheating or dropping voltage. * Ensures Signal Integrity: By mapping out current draws and using a clean linear regulator, I protect sensitive analog sensors and amplifiers from electrical noise that could ruin sensor readings. * Verifies Feasibility: It proves mathematically that my circuit design is safe, reliable, and ready for both benchtop laboratory testing and final enclosure assembly.

docs.title: Conclusions from the Prepared Power Budget
Summary of Findings
docs.text:
After completing and analyzing the power budget for the Light Sensing Subsystem, several key conclusions can be drawn:

  • Sufficient Power Delivery: The system requires a total active current of 22.5 mA, which increases to 28.125 mA after applying a standard 25% engineering safety margin. The selected 9V DC wall adapter (WSU090-1300-13) provides a 1300 mA capacity, leaving 300 mA of remaining headroom on the power source and ensuring the supply never experiences thermal overload or voltage sag.
  • Stable and Clean Regulation: By stepping down the incoming 9V supply using an L7805CV linear regulator onto a single regulated +5.0V power rail, my sensitive analog components (like the MCP6004 op-amp and photoresistor divider) receive steady DC power free from unwanted noise.
  • Feasible Portable Runtime: While intended primarily for desktop laboratory operation, calculations confirm that the circuit can be powered via a standard 9V alkaline battery (6LR61-1B, 480 mAh capacity) for roughly 21.33 hours of continuous runtime if field testing is ever required.

docs.title: Final Design Verdict
docs.text: My power distribution architecture is clean, efficient, and built with reliable, standard components. It avoids unnecessary circuit complexity while guaranteeing safe, stable performance for both benchtop testing and final enclosure integration.
